summary: Help 9-11 year-olds reframe gravity from the intuitive 'things fall down' to a directional, universal pulling force: Earth attracts every object toward its CENTRE, so 'down' is not a single fixed cosmic direction but 'toward the centre of the sphere' for everyone — which is why people all around the globe stay firmly on the ground and nobody falls off. The same long-reach pull holds the Moon in orbit around Earth and the planets around the Sun, acting across empty space with no need for air or contact. Keep it qualitative and directional at this age; reserve mass-vs-weight formalism and F=ma for later. Core misconceptions to confront: 'down' as absolute (so the far side falls off), 'no gravity in space', gravity needing air, gravity only acting on falling/unsupported things, and heavier objects always falling noticeably faster.
misconceptions: Thinking 'down' is a single absolute direction in the universe, so people on the 'other side' of the globe should fall off — not grasping that down means toward Earth's centre for everyone.
Believing there is NO gravity in space, or that astronauts float because gravity has switched off — rather than being in continual free-fall/orbit with gravity still acting.
Thinking gravity needs air (an atmosphere) to work, so it couldn't act in the vacuum of space or on the airless Moon.
Assuming gravity only acts on things that are falling or unsupported, not realising it acts on everything all the time (including things at rest and objects in orbit).
Not connecting the everyday 'falling' force with the force that holds the Moon and planets in orbit — treating them as unrelated.
Believing heavier objects are pulled much harder and so always fall noticeably faster (the Aristotelian attractor), ignoring air resistance as the real everyday difference.

activities.title: Everyone's 'down' points to the centre
steps: Using a globe (a physical ball, classroom globe, or an on-screen globe cross-section), place stick-figures all around it — top, sides, and the very bottom.
For each figure, draw or reveal a 'down' arrow from their feet and trace where it points; notice every arrow aims at the SAME place: the centre of the Earth.
Place one figure directly opposite yourself — standing 'upside-down' relative to you — and check that their 'down' still points to the middle.

On an on-screen model, use the drop-a-ball animation to release balls from several different positions and watch them all head inward toward the centre. On a physical globe, do this as a representational step instead — trace or draw each ball's path/arrow toward the model's centre — because real dropped balls fall toward the actual Earth, not toward a model globe's centre.
Answer aloud: 'If down means toward the centre, does anyone fall off? Why not?'
activities.insight: 'Down' is a local, radial direction — toward Earth's centre — not one fixed direction in the universe. Because every person's 'down' points to the centre, people all around the globe feel perfectly normal and nobody falls off, even though their 'down' points a different way in space from ours — and for someone directly opposite us, the opposite way.

activities.title: Same pull drops a ball and bends the Moon's path
steps: Study (or manipulate) a diagram of the Moon circling Earth with a gravity arrow pointing from the Moon toward Earth.

Predict: 'If the pull between Earth and Moon suddenly switched off, what path would the Moon take?' Then check in the simple Earth–Moon model (ignoring the Sun's pull) — with the pull off, the Moon moves off in a straight (tangent) line; with the pull on, that same pull curves its path into an orbit.
Repeat the idea with a Sun-at-centre diagram: each planet has a gravity arrow pointing at the Sun.
State in your own words how the force that drops a ball on Earth is the SAME force that keeps the Moon and planets in orbit.
Explain whether gravity needs air to work, using the airless Moon as evidence.
activities.insight: Gravity is a long-reach attraction acting across empty space — no air or contact needed. The same pull that makes a ball fall is what bends the Moon's straight-line motion into an orbit around Earth, and the planets' paths around the Sun.

activities.title: Busting the 'zero gravity' myth
steps: Look at an image of an astronaut floating and discuss WHY they float.
Decide which explanation fits the evidence: (a) gravity has switched off, or (b) the astronaut and their ship are both falling around Earth together, with Earth's gravity still strongly acting.
Connect this to the orbit idea: being in orbit IS continual free-fall around Earth.
Answer: 'Is there gravity where astronauts are? How do you know?'
activities.insight: Astronauts float because they are in continual free-fall (orbit) around Earth, where Earth's gravity is still strong — not because gravity has vanished. 'Weightlessness' is free-fall, not absence of gravity.

activities.title: Check and reason: which way is 'down'?
steps: Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'A child in Australia is on nearly the opposite side of the round Earth from a child in Britain. Are the people in Australia hanging upside down, in danger of falling off into space? What does "down" actually mean for them? Tell me WHY.'
Decide: is there one single 'down' for the whole universe, or does 'down' depend on where you're standing?
Match each cause to its effect: Earth's pull → a ball falls toward the centre; Earth's pull → the Moon orbits; the Sun's pull → planets orbit.
Judge true or false and justify: 'There is no gravity in space.'
activities.insight: Being able to explain WHY no one falls off — because 'down' is centre-relative, not absolute — is the crux. A learner who still holds an absolute 'down' thinks the far side hangs upside-down; a learner who understands the concept says everyone's feet point 'down' toward the centre and no one falls.

checkQuestion: A child in Australia is on the exact opposite side of the round Earth from a child in Britain. Are the people in Australia hanging upside down, in danger of falling off into space? What does 'down' actually mean for them? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: No — nobody falls off, because gravity pulls everything toward the CENTRE of the Earth, and 'down' means 'toward Earth's centre' wherever you stand. For the child in Australia, 'down' points to the centre just as it does in Britain, so their feet are firmly on the ground and everything feels perfectly normal — even though their 'down' points the opposite way in space to ours. There is no single fixed 'down' in the universe; each person's down points to Earth's centre. (That same pull, reaching across space, is what keeps the Moon orbiting Earth and the planets orbiting the Sun.)
